## Research Question 
Do diamonds with a color value of "E" have a different average price than diamonds with a color value of "I"?

## Hypotheses 
Null- The average price of diamonds with a color value of "E" is the same as diamonds with a color value of "I". 
Alternative- The average price of diamonds with a color value of "E" is different than diamonds with a color value of "I". 

## Checking normality
```{r}
library(tidyverse)
diamonds <- read.csv("diamonds 2.csv")
diamonds_filtered <- diamonds %>%
  filter(color %in% c("E", "I")) 

diamonds_plot <- diamonds_filtered %>%
  ggplot() + 
  geom_histogram(mapping = aes(x = price, fill = color), bins = 20, color = "white")
diamonds_plot
```
I wanted to compare a continuous outcome, so I ran a test on this dataset. This plot shows that diamond prices, regardless of the color, have a strong right skew. This tells us that the data is not normally distributed since there is not a bell-shaped curve, so we cannot use a t-test or a one-way ANOVA. Since there are only two groups, we cannot use a Kruskal-Wallis test, and the right test to use is a Wilcoxon rank-sum since there is a strong skew. 

## Running the Wilcoxon rank-sum test
```{r}
wilcox.test(price ~ color, data = diamonds_filtered)
```

## Written conclusion
I used a wilcoxon rank-sum test because my dataset, when plotted as a histogram, had a strong right skew. I also wanted to compare a continuous outcome between 2 groups, the price and the color grade of the diamonds rated "E" and "I", which affirmed my decision to use a wilcoxon rank-sum test. The p-value for this test was <2.2e-16. Based on this p-value, since it is below a significance level of 0.05, this provides evidence against the null hypothesis and indicates the data is inconsistent with the null hypothesis. To conclude, I was able to reject the null hypothesis that the price distribution of diamonds with a color value of "E" is the same as diamonds with a color value of "I". I might be making a type I error because I am rejecting the null hypothesis when it could actually be true. For example, I could conclude that color grade "E" and "I" diamonds have an difference in price distributions when in reality, they might be the same distribution, which would support the null hypothesis instead of reject it.
